title: Ramesh Kumar v. State of Rajasthan

facts: The appellant and two others attacked the deceased with sticks near the village well.
An FIR was registered under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC on the same evening.
issues: The question that arises is whether common intention under Section 34 was established against each accused.
arguments: Learned counsel for the appellant submitted that there was no prior meeting of minds.
reasoning: In our opinion common intention may develop on the spot and can be inferred from conduct.
The eye witnesses consistently described a joint attack.
decision: The appeal is dismissed and the conviction under Section 302/34 IPC is upheld.

title: Sunita Devi v. State of Haryana

facts: The wife died of burn injuries within four years of marriage in the matrimonial home.
Her parents alleged repeated demands for dowry and harassment by the husband.
issues: Whether the presumption under Section 113B of the Indian Evidence Act arises for a dowry death under Section 304B IPC.
arguments: It was contended for the accused that the death was accidental while cooking.
reasoning: We are of the view that cruelty soon before death was proved by consistent testimony.
Once the ingredients are shown the presumption of dowry death operates.
decision: In the result the conviction under Sections 304B and 498A IPC is affirmed.

title: Mehta Traders v. Gupta Enterprises

facts: The accused issued a cheque towards the price of goods which was returned unpaid for insufficient funds.
A complaint was filed u/s 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act after the statutory notice.
issues: The point for determination is whether the cheque was issued for a legally enforceable debt.
arguments: Learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that the cheque was given only as security.
reasoning: Having considered the record, the presumption under the Act was not rebutted by the accused.
decision: The revision petition is dismissed.

title: Anil Sharma v. Union of India

facts: The petitioner was detained under a preventive detention order without being told the grounds.
He challenged the detention by a writ of habeas corpus.
issues: Whether the procedure for detention satisfied Article 21 and Article 22 of the Constitution of India.
arguments: It was contended by the State that the detention was necessary for public order.
reasoning: In our opinion personal liberty under Art. 21 requires a procedure that is fair, just and reasonable.
decision: The detention order is quashed and we direct the release of the petitioner.

title: Vikram Singh v. State of Punjab

facts: The applicant has been in custody for two years awaiting trial in a robbery case.
His bail application under Section 439 Cr.P.C. was rejected by the Sessions Court.
issues: Whether prolonged custody without trial justifies grant of regular bail.
arguments: Learned counsel for the applicant submitted that the trial is unlikely to conclude soon.
reasoning: Speedy trial is part of personal liberty and long incarceration weighs in favour of bail.
decision: The application is allowed and the applicant is released on bail.

title: Commissioner of Income Tax v. Bharat Infra Ltd.

facts: The assessee developed a toll road and claimed deduction under Section 80-IA of the Income-tax Act, 1961.
The Assessing Officer disallowed the claim treating the assessee as a works contractor.
issues: Whether an infrastructure developer is entitled to deduction u/s 80IA when it also executes the construction.
arguments: It was contended by the Revenue that the assessee did not own the facility.
reasoning: We are of the view that a developer who bears the investment risk qualifies for the deduction.
decision: The appeal of the Revenue is dismissed.

title: Gopal Yadav v. State of Uttar Pradesh

facts: A sudden quarrel over irrigation water led to a fight in which the deceased received a single blow.
The trial court convicted the appellant for murder under Section 302 IPC.
issues: Whether the offence falls under Section 304 Part II IPC as culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
arguments: Learned counsel for the appellant submitted that there was no premeditation and only one blow.
reasoning: Having considered the circumstances, the act was done in a sudden fight without undue advantage.
decision: The appeal is partly allowed and the conviction is altered to Section 304 Part II IPC.

title: Harish Chand v. State of Madhya Pradesh

facts: The prosecution relied on a confession allegedly made by the accused to a police officer.
Statements of witnesses were recorded under Section 161 Cr.P.C. during investigation.
issues: Whether a confession made to a police officer is admissible in view of Section 25 of the Evidence Act.
arguments: It was contended for the State that the confession was voluntary.
reasoning: In our opinion a confession to a police officer is wholly inadmissible and cannot be used against the accused.
decision: The appeal is allowed and the appellant is acquitted.

title: Kamala Builders v. Ravi Prasad

facts: The defendant agreed to sell a plot and received part payment but refused to execute the sale deed.
The plaintiff sued for specific performance of the agreement.
issues: Whether the agreement was a valid contract under Section 10 of the Indian Contract Act enforceable by specific performance.
arguments: Learned counsel for the defendant submitted that the price was never finally agreed.
reasoning: Having considered the correspondence, there was a concluded contract and the plaintiff was ready and willing.
decision: The appeal is dismissed and the decree for specific performance is confirmed.

title: Lakshmi Bai v. State of Maharashtra

facts: The victim made a dying declaration before a Magistrate naming the accused as her assailant.
She died the next day of stab wounds and a case under Section 302 IPC was registered.
issues: Whether a dying declaration under Section 32 of the Evidence Act alone can sustain a conviction.
arguments: It was contended that the declarant was not in a fit state of mind.
reasoning: We are of the view that a truthful and voluntary dying declaration recorded by a Magistrate can form the sole basis of conviction.
decision: The appeal is dismissed.

title: Sharma Steel Ltd. v. Arora Finance

facts: A company cheque was dishonoured and the complainant prosecuted the company and all its directors.
The complaint invoked Sections 138 and 141 of the N.I. Act.
issues: Whether a non-executive director is vicariously liable under Section 141 without specific averments.
arguments: Learned counsel for the directors submitted that they were not in charge of the business.
reasoning: In our opinion the complaint must specifically aver how each director was responsible for the conduct of business.
decision: The appeal is allowed and the proceedings against the non-executive directors are quashed.

title: City Transport Co. v. State of Karnataka

facts: The State cancelled a tender after bids were opened and awarded the contract to a higher bidder.
The lowest bidder challenged the decision.
issues: Whether the cancellation was arbitrary and violative of Article 14 of the Constitution.
arguments: It was contended by the State that it reserved the right to reject any bid.
reasoning: We are of the view that State action in contracts must be fair and non-arbitrary.
decision: The writ petition is allowed.

title: Mohan Lal v. State of Gujarat

facts: The accused fired a country-made pistol at the complainant who escaped with a minor injury.
He was convicted for attempt to murder under Section 307 IPC.
issues: Whether intention to kill can be inferred when the injury caused is simple.
arguments: Learned counsel for the appellant submitted that the injury was only on the arm.
reasoning: The nature of the weapon and the manner of use show the intention irrespective of the injury.
decision: The appeal is dismissed.

title: Kapoor Estates v. Nandini Rao

facts: The landlord sought eviction of a tenant claiming bona fide need for his son's business.
The Rent Controller ordered eviction.
issues: Whether the landlord's requirement was bona fide under the Rent Control Act.
arguments: It was contended for the tenant that alternative premises were available.
reasoning: Having considered the evidence, the need was genuine and the landlord is the best judge of it.
decision: The revision is dismissed.

title: Rajesh Verma v. State of Bihar

facts: The deceased was last seen with the accused and his body was recovered the next morning.
There was no eye witness and the prosecution relied on circumstantial evidence for murder under Section 302 IPC.
issues: Whether the last seen circumstance with other circumstances forms a complete chain pointing only to guilt.
arguments: Learned counsel for the appellant submitted that the time gap was large.
reasoning: In our opinion the chain of circumstances must exclude every hypothesis except guilt.
decision: The appeal is allowed and the appellant is acquitted.

title: Priya Nair v. State of Kerala

facts: The wife alleged continuous cruelty and harassment by her husband and in-laws for dowry.
A case under Section 498A IPC was registered on her complaint.
issues: Whether general allegations against all in-laws are enough to proceed under Section 498A.
arguments: It was contended for the in-laws that they lived separately.
reasoning: We are of the view that specific acts of cruelty must be attributed to each accused.
decision: The petition is partly allowed.

title: Footpath Vendors Union v. Municipal Corporation

facts: The corporation removed street vendors without notice and seized their goods.
The vendors approached the Court under Article 32.
issues: Whether the right to livelihood is part of the right to life under Article 21.
arguments: It was contended by the corporation that pavements are meant for pedestrians.
reasoning: In our opinion the right to life includes the right to livelihood, subject to reasonable regulation.
decision: We direct the corporation to frame a scheme before any further removal.

title: Assistant Commissioner v. Coastal Ports Ltd.

facts: The assessee built and operated a port terminal and claimed deduction under Sec. 80IA of the Income Tax Act.
The deduction was denied on the ground that the terminal was not an infrastructure facility.
issues: Whether a port terminal operated under an agreement with the State qualifies as an infrastructure facility for Section 80-IA.
arguments: Learned counsel for the assessee submitted that ports are expressly included in the definition.
reasoning: Having considered the provision, a port terminal is an infrastructure facility and the deduction is available.
decision: The appeal of the assessee is allowed.

title: Arjun Malhotra v. State (NCT of Delhi)

facts: The applicant apprehended arrest in a cheating case registered by the police.
He sought anticipatory bail under Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
issues: Whether anticipatory bail must be limited in time.
arguments: It was contended for the State that custodial interrogation was necessary.
reasoning: We are of the view that liberty under Art. 21 does not permit an inflexible time limit on anticipatory bail.
decision: The appeal is allowed and anticipatory bail is granted.

title: Deepak Agencies v. Sai Distributors

facts: The complainant sent the demand notice for a dishonoured cheque but filed the complaint after the period of limitation.
The complaint was made u/s 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act.
issues: Whether delay in filing the complaint can be condoned under Section 142.
arguments: Learned counsel for the complainant submitted that sufficient cause was shown.
reasoning: Having considered the proviso, the court may condone delay on sufficient cause.
decision: The petition is allowed and the delay is condoned.
